hypotheses.measurement: Admission ledger (owner, volume, data) plus task-mining clusters over the flagship and gateway logs
hypotheses.confirmedIf: By the end of wave 1, servicing (Advice), Compliance and Judge each hold three or more admitted purposes with named owners
hypotheses.refutedIf: A domain holds one or fewer admitted purposes after a quarter; TL-011 should not carry it as a Domain model

hypotheses.claim: H2 (lab, near-circular). Most multi-model agents are Core plus a judge, so the Judge family is the shared dependency and the first platform build
hypotheses.measurement: Model recipe per admitted purpose; demand counts in the capability catalogue
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 70% or more of admitted multi-model purposes carry a judge component and the Judge family holds the highest demand count
hypotheses.refutedIf: Fewer than half carry one, or deterministic checks replace the judge in most

hypotheses.claim: H3 (lab, proxy). Methodology variants of one purpose differ enough that the choice matters, and the simplest variant does not always win
hypotheses.measurement: Each wave-1 purpose in two variants x two levels on declared public or synthetic data, paired tests, 3+ seeds: house rubric, cost per task, latency, pass^k
hypotheses.confirmedIf: For at least two purposes, variants differ by more than 5 rubric points, or by 2x on cost at equal quality
hypotheses.refutedIf: Variants within 3 points and 1.5x cost on all purposes: stop building variants, ship the simplest build (kill criterion I-5)

hypotheses.claim: H4 (lab, provisional). The winning variant on TLM4 Core with the house judge matches a frontier baseline at lower cost, with data inside the boundary
hypotheses.measurement: Same inputs and frontier-panel judge for both arms, plus a human-graded audit by Jithin (one grader, disclosed)
hypotheses.confirmedIf: Within 3 points of the frontier at half the cost or less
hypotheses.refutedIf: The frontier leads by more than 3 points after one retrain cycle; that purpose is not evidence for a Domain model

hypotheses.claim: H5 (company version). A compared, adoptable variant is picked up by a business team without ThinkLatent engineering
hypotheses.measurement: Teams using a library variant within 60 days of publication; time from request to first use
hypotheses.confirmedIf: Two or more teams adopt a wave-1 purpose within 60 days; first use inside two weeks
hypotheses.refutedIf: No adoption outside the originating team

hypotheses.claim: H6 (company version). Wave 1 reduces human time on its two business purposes without losing recall
hypotheses.measurement: After-call minutes per call; pre-review reviewer minutes per item and recall on known true positives, frozen pre/post window
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 30% less after-call time; 40% less reviewer time at no loss of recall
hypotheses.refutedIf: No change, or recall drops; the agent is withdrawn from that queue

hypotheses.claim: H7 (lab, narrowed). A change of harness or serving configuration moves pass^k materially on one Core version; the Core-version comparison waits for the company version
hypotheses.measurement: Each wave-1 purpose across two serving configurations on one pinned Core version, pass^k on the index
hypotheses.confirmedIf: The serving-configuration delta exceeds 5 pass^k points on at least two purposes
hypotheses.refutedIf: Serving-configuration deltas sit within noise; harness variants are not worth a stream

hypotheses.claim: H8 (company version). Shown quality, cost, latency and reliability side by side, business teams choose variants on the measured frontier
hypotheses.measurement: The index logs each team's choice beside the comparison card
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 70% or more of choices sit on the accuracy-cost frontier
hypotheses.refutedIf: Choices cluster on a dominated variant; the comparison card is redesigned

Portal direction. Why we build it: to express the collective intelligence of the organisation, at institution level, by embedding it in models, which no frontier lab offers; once embedded, teams use the models for new use cases, those generate interaction data and feedback, and the business intelligence compounds. The portal must let people see that compounding without being told. The portal is organised around models and use cases, not roles: the model is the core pillar (foundation model, domain model built from it, use case on top, with versions that move together); the only thing tied to people is membership of a use case, given by adding a company email; everything the Head sees is open to everyone, including a leaderboard of use cases by usage and value. Every number links to the page behind it. The prototype is the full requirement for the next year: build everything, do not cut for timeline or role; hiding comes later as an option. Each request and each call inside it is a signal to capture and show. This supersedes the role workspaces of D-219 to D-222 and the role lens in D-234

(1) 'Model' means every kind of model, not only language models: TLM1-generation classifiers built on BERT, the speech-recognition network that processes about 150,000 calls a day, redaction, guardrails, embeddings, rerankers (Claude's reading of 'reversion model', not yet confirmed), and models that work in the background; more as applications evolve. (2) Many to many: a model serves many projects and one project uses several models, as different jobs in one flow, as separate features, as old and new side by side, and as agents that bring a model. (3) The project carries the stage and is delivered in increments: new models for new tasks are added at any time, increments run in parallel, and each goes to production on its own approval. (4) Each kind of model is scored on its own measure with a bar and a leaderboard of its kind; the TL Index stays for language models. (5) A shared model is handled both ways: Enterprise-wide work is one project for the Enterprise, and the same model can also sit inside another project for its own purpose (speech in an application's interface, redaction as a support function). (6) Hierarchy, in Jithin's words: Organization, Team, Project, Feature (for example Retail Business, Advice Tech, Advisor desktop, then call summary, next best action, speech to text; the same team can hold a second project), with models under features. The names and where membership sits are still being settled. Where a board assumes roles or one model per project, this vision wins and the board guides layout only (amends D-247).

Vision, continued (follows D-249). (1) Levels: Organization, Team, Project, Feature, with models under features; a project carries its team as owner and can move teams without losing its history (Claude's caution, not yet confirmed). (2) Membership: people join a project; a team's owners can open and manage every project the team holds; everyone else gets the open view. (3) Rule for the whole navigation: every level shows the breakdown of the level below it, and the detail (traces, sessions, operations) lives at the project; a model's page shows improvement, API calls and tokens, adoption and value. (4) Two-level navigation, option A, chosen from three drawn options (canvas 'navigation options'): the approved dock stays and gets shorter; a clickable scope bar says where you are (Organization, Team, Project, Feature); tabs under the title change with the level. (5) Home is a cockpit, not one list: TLM model adoption and what is running in production today by stage; usage by kind; an adoption and usage leaderboard at team level with a double-click into a team's projects; and the AI agent in front, which understands the ask, brings the information and routes the person to the right place, flattening the path from onboarding to approvals. (6) Jithin's ask for what follows: Claude keeps asking questions one at a time until the vision is clear, then designs the UX and UI in the approved design and draws it by hand so it fits; nothing more is built until then.

Vision, continued (follows D-250). (1) Usage by kind of work comes off Home for now and is parked for later as a Home exhibit; Home keeps models live by kind and requests split into live and background. (2) Approvals sit outside the portal, for projects and for models alike. A deployment triggers a workflow in the Enterprise's change system and the change request is approved by the ThinkLatent team; model approval is also recorded in an outside system. The portal prepares the evidence, raises the request and shows its status; it approves nothing. The approver queues and hold-to-approve screens for use cases and validations on the earlier boards become request status. (3) The model catalogue is grouped by generation first (TLM1 to TLM5), with the kinds of model inside each. (4) Budgets are held by the team; spend and value are counted per project and feature and roll up to team and organization. (5) Taken as settled unless Jithin says otherwise: the agent on Home is one line at the top of the cockpit (Claude's recommendation after Jithin asked for analysis); 'reversion model' is read as reranker.

On the first draft of the Home cockpit ('looks good', with three changes). (1) No budgets in the portal: budget detail will not be available, so the portal shows spend and what was saved, meaning cost avoided for the company; this reverses item 4 of D-251. (2) The flow from models to teams leaves Home: it is good but falls apart beyond about ten models; the space becomes a quick model catalogue, tiles that open each model's page, with what is new and coming (releases, retraining, editions) beside it. The mapping of models to teams and projects stays on each model's and each team's page. (3) Tokens are the common unit across every kind of model, speech included: input and output tokens are shown for each model, and the overall tokens in and out sit at the title level of Home to show the scale. Second draft drawn with these on the canvas.

The second draft of the Home cockpit is accepted ('looking good, continue'): the agent line, running now, a quick model catalogue with what is new and coming, teams ranked by adoption with spend and cost avoided, and tokens in and out at the title and on each model. Claude continues drawing the rest of the structure on the canvas in the same way, one screen at a time: a model's page is drafted next (scope bar All models, generation, model, version; its measure, adoption, improvement by version, what it is built from, where it is used with its job in each feature, tokens by day).

Four more libraries go into the kit as owned source on kit tokens, so every product can use and change them freely: Beautiful UI (MIT, from a public mirror of the site's code), Bencho's free blocks (MIT), BoardUI's free set (MIT, kept on React Aria, Remix icons swapped for Lucide) and the 36 free Transitions.dev transitions. Transitions.dev has a custom licence that forbids republishing the collection as a kit: allowed as a recorded exception on the condition that the kit stays private and is never published, sold or given away, its comment stays on each transition, and no Pro transitions are taken. Paid tiers of Bencho, BoardUI and Transitions.dev are not taken. design-kit v0.8.0 (cdebcec): 2,514 of 2,539 usable, 25 excluded, none blocked

The first draft of a model's page is accepted ('continue, it looks good'). Drawn next on the same canvas, for his review: a project's page (Advisor desktop: scope bar organization, team, project, feature; its features with the models in each in the order they run, tokens and score against its bar per feature; increments with the status of each change request, approved outside the portal; members; traces, sessions and operations at project level) and the Models catalogue by generation (TLM5 to TLM1, kinds inside, one row a model with its version and state, its own measure against its bar, where it is used, calls and tokens in and out). Sample totals now add up across the boards: 2.3B tokens in, 208M out across nine live models. Open with Jithin: what TLM2 held, and whether the split of kinds across generations is right.

portfolio.diagnosis: The constraint on ThinkLatent is not model quality but evidence for adoption and governance throughput: owned models exist, and nothing proves to the business and Risk that they are sufficient and safe for a given workflow. Ideas that relieve this constraint come first.

spine.winningAspiration: Every model decision at the Enterprise runs on evidence, and most AI work runs on models the Enterprise owns, inside its own boundary, at lower cost and with clearer governance than renting frontier models by default.
spine.whereToPlay: Bounded, high-volume workflows (extraction, classification, routing, servicing, compliance pre-review) on Enterprise-built specialists; frontier models only where measured evidence shows a gain worth paying for. Not: general-purpose chat products, or competing with vendors on frontier capability.
spine.howToWin: Evidence nobody else has (the index on Enterprise tasks), an owned build-and-heal loop (TLM, compression, self-healing), and a governance path that approves usages faster than the side door.
